title: Inito Estrogen Trends Throughout the Cycle: What Your E3G Levels Mean
summary: Learn how estrogen changes throughout your cycle, what different Inito estrogen chart trends can indicate, and how E3G helps identify your fertile window.
body_markdown:
Estrogen can tell you a lot about where you are in your cycle, especially when ovulation is getting closer. As your follicles grow and mature, estrogen levels begin to rise. And on your Inito chart, this rise in estrogen can help identify the start of your fertile window.
But estrogen doesn’t always follow the exact same pattern from one cycle to another. You may see it rise earlier or later, fluctuate before Peak Fertility, or rise again after ovulation. **So, what do all these different estrogen patterns actually mean?**
In this article, we’ll walk through common estrogen trends on Inito throughout the follicular phase, around ovulation, and during the luteal phase. We’ll also look at variations you may see on your chart and what they can tell you about your cycle.
**(Note: Inito measures 4 key fertility hormones in urine: LH, estrogen, PdG (urine metabolite of progesterone), and FSH.)**


## Key Takeaways


- Estrogen typically rises in the mid-to-late follicular phase as follicles grow, making it an early sign that ovulation is approaching.
- A significant rise in estrogen from your baseline helps Inito identify High Fertility.
- Estrogen usually starts rising 3-4 days before the LH surge, dips after ovulation, and may show a smaller second rise during the luteal phase.
- Your estrogen pattern may not follow the textbook trend every cycle. You may see more or fewer High Fertility days, fluctuations, or different E3G levels from one cycle to the next.
- Focus on trends rather than individual estrogen values. What matters is how estrogen changes alongside LH and PdG and whether ovulation is ultimately confirmed.
- If you repeatedly notice unusual hormone patterns or ovulation isn’t being confirmed, consider discussing your charts with your healthcare provider.


## How Does Inito Track Estrogen?


Inito tracks a urine metabolite of estrogen called E3G (estrone-3-glucuronide). After estrogen is metabolized by your body, some of it is excreted in urine as E3G. E3G[closely follows changes in estrogen levels](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.3109/13625187.2015.1048331) in the body, making it useful for tracking how estrogen changes throughout your cycle.


This is especially helpful as you approach ovulation. As your follicles grow and mature, they produce more estrogen. This rise typically begins **before the LH surge** , making it an early sign that ovulation is approaching.


When Inito detects a significant rise in estrogen from your baseline, it marks **High Fertility** , letting you know that your fertile window has begun. And when LH rises, Inito marks **Peak Fertility** .


**Read more:[Differences Between High Fertility and Peak Fertility](https://blog.inito.com/differences-between-high-fertility-and-peak-fertility/)**


So, the pattern on your Inito chart may look like:


**Estrogen rises → High Fertility → LH surges → Peak Fertility → PdG rises → Ovulation Confirmed**


**Note** : Estrogen levels vary from person to person, so Inito looks for a rise from your own unique baseline to identify High Fertility. Your hormone trend matters more than comparing a single estrogen value.


## What Do Estrogen Trends Typically Look Like Throughout the Menstrual Cycle?


A textbook estrogen pattern generally looks something like this:


**Phase**


**How estrogen typically behaves**


**Early follicular phase**


Estrogen is usually relatively low at the beginning of your cycle.


**Mid to late follicular phase**


Estrogen rises as your follicles grow and mature.


**Around ovulation**


Estrogen typically starts to rise 3-4 days before the LH surge, helping trigger the release of the egg.


**Luteal phase**


Estrogen dips after ovulation; it may show a smaller second rise alongside progesterone in the mid-luteal phase.


**Keep in mind:** These are generalized estrogen trends, and your E3G pattern may not look exactly like this. We’ll explore common variations (and what they may mean) within each phase below.


## Follicular Phase: What Happens to Estrogen at the Beginning of Your Cycle?


At the beginning of the follicular phase, estrogen is generally relatively low. As your ovarian follicles develop, they begin producing more estrogen, causing levels to gradually increase as you get closer to ovulation.
**A quick note before we get into the charts:** We’ve recreated each example using representative hormone patterns so you can easily see the trend we’re talking about. These are not actual user charts.


### **Estrogen trends lower at the beginning of the cycle (“textbook trend”)**


In this chart, you can see that estrogen is low at the beginning of the cycle.
This is the pattern you may expect to see in a textbook cycle.
During the early follicular phase, several follicles begin developing. As a dominant follicle emerges and continues to mature, it produces increasing amounts of estrogen, which is why estrogen starts rising in the mid-to-late follicular phase.


### **Estrogen seems to trend higher at the beginning of the cycle (variation)**


Sometimes, your estrogen may already appear at a higher trend or elevated when you begin testing in a new cycle. And this could be because hormone levels from the previous cycle haven’t fully returned to their baseline yet.


### **Estrogen starts rising earlier in the follicular phase (variation)**


Sometimes, an earlier estrogen rise simply means your follicles are developing earlier in that particular cycle, and[ovulation may happen earlier too](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC27529/) . This means you have shorter cycles.
Remember, the follicular phase is the more variable part of your cycle, so the timing of your estrogen rise (and therefore your fertile window) can shift from one cycle to another. Rather than focusing on which cycle day estrogen “should” rise, look at how estrogen changes compared to your baseline levels.


## Ovulation: What Happens to Estrogen Before Egg Release?


Estrogen rises significantly as the dominant follicle matures and typically reaches its highest levels around 3-4 days before ovulation. Sustained raised estrogen creates a positive feedback loop that helps trigger the LH surge, which then sets ovulation in motion.


Research shows that estrogen typically peaks shortly before or around the LH surge. In fact, one study found that in nearly 90% of cycles,[estrogen reached its peak right before or at the same time as the LH surge.](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0015028207001604)


This is especially useful because catching the estrogen rise can give you an earlier heads-up that your fertile window has begun–and more days to try.
But this pattern doesn’t always look the same on every chart. Let’s look at a few variations you might see.


### **Estrogen rises before the LH surge (“textbook trend”)**


This is the classic pattern you may expect.
First, estrogen rises enough from baseline for Inito to mark **High Fertility** . A few days later, LH surges and Inito marks **Peak Fertility** .


This gives you several fertile days leading up to ovulation instead of waiting until the LH surge to know that ovulation is approaching.


**Note:** Estrogen doesn’t always move in a straight line. It often rises and dips from one day to the next, creating a wave-like pattern. In some cycles, though, you may see a smoother, more gradual rise or fall.


### **I went straight to Peak Fertility without seeing High Fertility**


**


**


Sometimes, you may see Peak Fertility without getting any High Fertility days first. A few reasons this can happen include:


- Your E3G didn’t show a significant rise from your baseline.
- Your LH surged earlier than expected.
- You may have missed a few tests at the beginning of your cycle, which can affect your fertility ratings.


**What does this mean?**


Going straight to Peak Fertility doesn’t necessarily mean something is wrong. Peak Fertility means Inito has detected your LH surge, indicating that ovulation is approaching. Continue testing so Inito can track PdG afterward and confirm whether ovulation occurred.


**Know more:[Early Ovulation: Symptoms, Causes, Treatment, and More](https://blog.inito.com/early-ovulation/)**


### **I only got one day of High Fertility before Peak Fertility**


Sometimes estrogen takes a little longer to show a sufficient rise from baseline, and then LH surges soon afterward.
In this chart, the user’s estrogen rise marks High Fertility, but their LH surge follows quickly, resulting in just one High Fertility day before Peak Fertility.
So, depending on when your estrogen begins to rise and a subsequent LH surge, you may get High Fertility days accordingly. Sometimes it is possible that you may get 2-3 days of High Fertility before your LH surge.


**What does this mean?**


This doesn’t necessarily mean your fertile window was only one day long. It simply reflects the hormone pattern Inito detected during that cycle.
The important next step is to continue testing so you can see whether PdG rises after the LH surge and ovulation is confirmed.


## Luteal Phase: What Happens to Estrogen After Ovulation?


After ovulation, estrogen usually dips temporarily[before showing a smaller, secondary rise during the mid-luteal phase](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6888463/) . This second rise often happens in[parallel to progesterone](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279054/) (Inito measures PdG, which is the urine metabolite of progesterone). Estrogen and progesterone work together during this phase to support the uterus as your body prepares for the possibility of implantation.


### **Why is my estrogen rising again alongside PdG? (“textbook trend”)**


Here, estrogen falls after its pre-ovulatory peak and then rises again during the luteal phase.
In this chart, you’ll also notice PdG rising during this time. That’s because after ovulation, the follicle that released the egg transforms into the corpus luteum. The corpus luteum produces progesterone as well as estrogen, which is why the two hormones can rise in parallel during the luteal phase.


### **Why don’t I see an estrogen rise after ovulation?**


Sometimes, luteal phase estrogen patterns can be more subtle, fluctuate from day to day, or look different from the textbook example.
So, instead of using the presence or absence of a secondary estrogen rise to determine whether you ovulated, look at your PdG pattern.
Inito confirms ovulation by looking for a sustained rise in PdG after your LH surge–not by requiring a particular luteal-phase estrogen pattern.


### **My estrogen stays elevated throughout the luteal phase**


You may also notice that estrogen stays relatively elevated rather than showing a clear dip followed by a second rise. Estrogen patterns during the luteal phase vary. What’s more useful is looking at your estrogen alongside your LH and PdG trends and comparing the overall pattern across multiple cycles.


**Note:** Inito can help you understand your hormone patterns and confirm ovulation, but it can’t be used to diagnose a hormonal condition or confirm pregnancy.


## How Should You Interpret Estrogen Patterns on Your Inito Chart?


When you’re tracking fertility with Inito, estrogen is most useful when you look at it as part of a sequence rather than as a standalone number.
Here’s what the main changes on your chart can tell you:


**Estrogen starts rising from baseline → High Fertility** : Your fertile window has likely begun. If you’re trying to conceive, this is a good time to start timing intercourse.
**LH surges → Peak Fertility:** Ovulation is approaching, and these are among your most fertile days.
**Peak Fertility has passed → keep testing:** Rather than continuing to focus only on timing intercourse, watch for a steady and consistent PdG rise.
**PdG rises sufficiently → Ovulation Confirmed:** Your hormone pattern indicates that ovulation occurred.


The main takeaway? Don’t let one estrogen number make or break your day.


**Your trend, how estrogen changes from your baseline, and what your other hormones do afterward provide much more context than one isolated value.**


## Why Do Estrogen Trends on Inito Look Different From Cycle to Cycle?


Your estrogen levels and trends may look different from one cycle to the next—and that can be expected. Estrogen is influenced by follicle development, as well as factors that can affect your cycle and the timing of ovulation.
Here are a few reasons your estrogen pattern may vary:


**Factor**


**How it may affect estrogen trends**


**Natural cycle variation**


Follicles may develop at a different pace, changing when and how estrogen rises.


**Stress or illness**


Can temporarily affect hormone signaling and shift the timing of ovulation. Higher daily stress was associated with


[9.5% lower estradiol levels](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4315337/) compared with lower daily stress.


**Travel or sleep changes**


Changes to your routine may temporarily affect your cycle and hormone patterns. Research suggests that


[sleep duration and sleep regularity are associated with estradiol levels](https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12958-022-00889-3) . One study found that women with more regular sleep schedules had 60% lower estradiol concentrations than women with irregular sleep schedules. Longer sleep duration was also associated with slightly higher average estradiol.


**PCOS**


You may see E3G rise and fall multiple times as follicles develop without immediately leading to ovulation.


**Coming off hormonal birth control**


E3G patterns may look different while your natural hormone signaling and ovulation resume.


**And sometimes, your E3G pattern can vary even when you ovulate in both cycles.**


**


**


In the first chart, there were 4 days of High Fertility, and after Peak Fertility, estrogen appeared to trend alongside PdG. In the next chart, estrogen generally stayed on the lower side, with 3 days of High Fertility before Peak Fertility. Despite these differences in estrogen patterns, both cycles showed Peak Fertility followed by confirmed ovulation.


**The takeaway:** Your E3G values don’t need to look identical every cycle. Instead of comparing individual numbers, look at the overall pattern—whether E3G rises as you approach your fertile window, followed by an LH surge and a PdG rise to confirm ovulation.


## When Should You Consider Seeing a Doctor About Your Estrogen Patterns?


Consider discussing your cycle and hormone patterns with your healthcare provider if you notice changes that persist across multiple cycles, particularly if you also have irregular periods or aren’t ovulating.
This may include:


- No clear estrogen rise across multiple cycles
- Repeated estrogen rises without subsequent ovulation
- Significant fluctuations that repeatedly don’t progress to an LH surge and ovulation
- Very irregular or absent periods
- A persistent change from your usual cycle pattern that concerns you


And if you’re trying to conceive, fertility evaluation is generally recommended after **12 months of trying if you’re under 35** , or after **6 months if you’re 35 or older.** Depending on your medical history or cycle patterns, your healthcare provider may recommend evaluation sooner.


**


**


Bring your cycle and hormone trends with you. Your Inito charts can’t diagnose the cause of an unusual hormone pattern, but they can give your healthcare provider additional context about what you’ve been seeing across your cycles.


## Conclusion


Estrogen is one of the earliest hormones to signal that your fertile window is approaching. On Inito, a rise in estrogen from your baseline helps identify High Fertility before the LH surge marks Peak Fertility.
But your estrogen chart doesn’t need to look exactly like a textbook example.
Estrogen may rise earlier or later; you may have only one High Fertility day before Peak Fertility, or you may see different luteal-phase patterns from one cycle to another.
Instead of focusing on whether one estrogen value looks “right,” follow the full hormone story: **estrogen rising, LH surging, and PdG rising afterward to confirm ovulation.**
And perhaps most importantly, compare **your patterns with your own previous cycles,** rather than someone else’s numbers. Over time, this can help you understand what your typical estrogen pattern looks like.
